case_name: CASE OF PENTIKÄINEN v. FINLAND
summary:
The applicant, Markus Veikko Pentikäinen, born in 1980 and living in Helsinki, is a photographer and journalist employed by the weekly magazine *Suomen Kuvalehti*. On 9 September 2006 he was sent by his employer to photograph the “Smash ASEM” demonstration in Helsinki, held in protest against the Asia-Europe Meeting. He was to report for the magazine’s print edition and publish online once the demonstration ended.

Before the event, Finnish Security Intelligence assessed the demonstration as hostile and without a clear political message. The police had difficulty contacting the organisers. Two earlier Helsinki demonstrations that year had turned violent. The announced march was to run from the Kiasma Museum to near the ASEM summit venue. Posters invited participants to wear black and referred to bringing “mayhem” to Helsinki’s streets.

The demonstration began at 6 p.m. About 500 bystanders, a core group of demonstrators, and some 50 journalists gathered. Violence soon broke out: bottles, stones, and paint-filled jars were thrown at police and the public. Police cordoned the area, announced that a peaceful demonstration was allowed but not a march, and later declared the event a riot. From 6.30 p.m. to 7.17 p.m. they sealed off the area. Police allowed families and media representatives to pass through, though projectiles were thrown at times. They repeatedly ordered the crowd to disperse. The applicant claimed he first heard the order around 8.30 p.m. and understood it as applying only to demonstrators. He called his employer and decided to stay. Around 9 p.m. a police officer told him personally he had one last chance to leave. The applicant said he was reporting for *Suomen Kuvalehti* and would follow the event to the end; the officer left him alone.

Later, police broke up remaining demonstrators and apprehended protesters. The applicant claimed he heard an officer shout, “Get the photographer!” He was taking photographs when apprehended. He told the officer he was a journalist and presented his press card; the officer later confirmed this. The applicant did not resist. The stated basis for apprehension was contumacy towards police. He was taken to a detention bus and then a police station, where he said he again identified himself as a journalist and wore his press card visibly. He claimed his camera equipment and memory cards were confiscated. The Government maintained that once police learned he was press, his equipment was treated as journalistic material and not confiscated; he retained the photographs. A Deputy Parliamentary Ombudsman report noted that police checked detainees’ mobile phones, though it was unclear whether the applicant’s phone or memory cards were inspected.

The applicant was detained from 9 September at 9.26 p.m. until 10 September at 3.05 p.m., about seventeen and a half hours. He was interrogated on 10 September between 1.32 p.m. and 1.57 p.m. Police apprehended 128 people in total; most were released on 11 September. The applicant was the seventh detainee interrogated and the sixth released after minors.

On 23 May 2007 the public prosecutor charged the applicant with contumacy towards the police under Chapter 16, section 4(1), of the Penal Code. On 17 December 2007 Helsinki District Court found him guilty but waived punishment under Chapter 6, section 12(3), treating the offence as comparable to an excusable act because of conflicting expectations from police and his profession. The court found police orders lawful, clear, and applicable to everyone, and concluded that restricting his freedom of expression was justified. The applicant appealed, arguing his apprehension and conviction violated the Constitution and Article 10. On 30 April 2009 the Court of Appeal dismissed the appeal without further reasons. On 1 September 2009 the Supreme Court refused leave to appeal.

The applicant alleged before the European Court that his Article 10 rights were violated because police ordered him to leave, he could not transmit information during his detention, and he was suspected, charged, and convicted, creating a chilling effect on his work.

case_name: CASE OF FERNÁNDEZ MARTÍNEZ v. SPAIN
summary:
José Antonio Fernández Martínez, a Spanish national born in 1937 and living in Cieza, was ordained a Catholic priest in 1961. In 1984 he asked the Vatican for dispensation from celibacy; receiving no immediate answer, he married civilly in 1985 and later had five children. From October 1991 he worked as a teacher of Catholic religion and ethics at a State-run secondary school in Murcia under renewable one-year contracts. Under a 1979 Spain–Holy See Agreement and a 1982 Ministerial Order, such teachers were appointed annually by the education authority from candidates proposed by the diocesan Ordinary; appointments renewed automatically unless the Ordinary objected or the authority annulled them for serious academic or disciplinary reasons.

In November 1996, the Murcian newspaper La Verdad published an article about the Movement for Optional Celibacy of priests (MOCEOP). It named the applicant among married priests who had gathered at La Luz to advocate optional celibacy and a more democratic Church. By a rescript of 20 August 1997, the Pope granted the applicant dispensation from celibacy. He lost clerical status and was barred from teaching Catholic religion in public institutions unless the local bishop decided otherwise for lower-level schools, provided there was no scandal. He was notified on 15 September 1997. On 29 September 1997 the Diocese of Cartagena informed the Ministry of Education that his service should end. On 9 October 1997 the Ministry informed him that his employment had terminated with effect from 29 September 1997. In a memorandum of 11 November 1997, the Diocese said his situation had become public and the bishop could no longer sign the authorisation; it also cited avoiding scandal, parents’ sensitivity, and his entitlement to unemployment benefit. The school’s board expressed support for him.

In domestic proceedings, his administrative complaint was unsuccessful, and an administrative court dismissed his appeal on 30 June 2000, finding that termination was the only course once the Diocese had not proposed him. He then brought an unfair-dismissal claim before Murcia Employment Tribunal no. 3. By judgment of 28 September 2000, the tribunal found he had been discriminated against because of his marital status and MOCEOP membership, declared the dismissal null and void, and ordered reinstatement and salary. On appeal, the Murcia High Court of Justice, by judgment of 26 February 2001, allowed the appeal. It considered the teacher-bishop relationship one based on trust, found no violation of the Spanish Constitution’s provisions on equality, freedom of thought and religion, private and family life, or freedom of expression, and held that the contract was temporary and had expired rather than being a dismissal.

The applicant lodged an amparo appeal, alleging violations of Articles 14, 18 and 20 of the Spanish Constitution. He argued that non-renewal because he had publicised his MOCEOP membership and dissenting views on priestly celibacy unjustifiably interfered with his private life and religious freedom. The public prosecutor supported the amparo, noting that his public appearance predated the rescript and that his MOCEOP membership had been known. By judgment of 4 June 2007, served on 18 June 2007, the Constitutional Court dismissed the amparo. It found no discrimination on marital-status grounds; no private-life violation because he had voluntarily made his situation public; and, balancing the Catholic Church’s religious freedom and parents’ rights, it regarded the reasons as religious and the measure as not disproportionate. Two judges dissented. A later nullity request, alleging two judges’ Catholic affinities, was rejected on 23 July 2007. On 11 December 2007 the applicant lodged application no. 56030/07 with the European Court of Human Rights, relying on Article 8 alone and with Article 14, and alleging that publicity about his family and personal situation as a married priest caused the non-renewal, incompatibly with Articles 9 and 10.

case_name: CASE OF BOUYID v. BELGIUM
summary:
The applicants, Saïd and Mohamed Bouyid, Belgian nationals born in 1986 and 1979 respectively, are brothers living with their family in Saint-Josse-ten-Noode, next to the local police station. They alleged that they were each slapped in the face by police officers at that station—one on 8 December 2003 and the other on 23 February 2004—against a background of tense relations between their family and certain officers. The Government disputed both allegations.

As to 8 December 2003, the applicants submitted that, at around 4 p.m., the first applicant was outside his building with a friend, ringing the bell because he had forgotten his keys. A plain-clothes officer, A.Z., asked to see his identity card. The first applicant refused and asked to see A.Z.’s credentials. A.Z. then grabbed him by his jacket, tearing it, and took him to the police station. There, while alone with A.Z. in a room, the officer allegedly slapped him in the face as he protested about his arrest. A medical certificate issued at 7.20 p.m. the same day stated that the first applicant was “in a state of shock” and noted “erythema on the left cheek (disappearing)” and “erythema on the left-side external auditory canal.” The Government submitted that, because the first applicant refused to show his identity card, A.Z. had no choice but to take him to the station for identification. It said the first applicant caused a scene, insulted an officer, and was released after identity checks; he was told a report would be filed for forceful resistance, abusive behaviour and verbal threats. He later returned with his parents accusing A.Z. of slapping him, which A.Z. denied. At 6 p.m. A.Z. lodged a criminal complaint against him.

As to 23 February 2004, the applicants submitted that between 9.44 a.m. and 10.20 a.m., while the second applicant was being interviewed by Officer P.P. at the station about an altercation involving him and his mother and a third party, P.P. asked him not to lean on his desk and then slapped him in the face. He allegedly forced him to sign his statement by threatening to place him in a cell. A medical certificate issued that day recorded “bruising [on the] left cheek”; it was presented to the Standing Committee for the oversight of police services (“Committee P”) before 11.20 a.m. The Government described the second applicant as arrogant during the interview—slouching, leaning on the desk, laughing, giving pithy answers—and said he changed his statement and threatened the officers on leaving. It stated that P.P. remained calm and patient, admitted grabbing the applicant by the arm to make him leave, but denied slapping him.

The first applicant complained to Committee P at 9.42 a.m. on 9 December 2003; the second complained at 11.20 a.m. on 23 February 2004. Their mother was also interviewed on 23 February 2004 and filed a complaint concerning P.P.’s attitude. On 5 May 2004, P.P. was interviewed by the internal oversight director and denied slapping the second applicant. On 17 June 2004, the applicants applied to intervene as civil parties in respect of harassment, arbitrary interference with fundamental freedoms, abuse of authority, arbitrary arrest and wounding with intent, expressly relying on the events of 8 December 2003 and 23 February 2004. Officers A.Z. and P.P. were charged with using violence against individuals in the course of their duties, intentional wounding or assault, and arbitrary acts. After a judicial investigation, the Crown Prosecutor sought discontinuance on 10 November 2005, and the Committals Division of the Brussels Court of First Instance discontinued the proceedings on 27 November 2007. On 9 April 2008, the Indictments Division of the Brussels Court of Appeal upheld the discontinuance, referring to inconsistent statements, lack of evidence, and a Committee P report on the family’s general conduct. The Court of Cassation dismissed an appeal on points of law on 29 October 2008. Separately, on 5 February 2008, six family members, including the applicants, filed a civil-party complaint about earlier facts; in a judgment of 30 May 2012, the Brussels Court of First Instance declared prosecution of those offences time-barred, and no appeal appears to have been lodged. The Strasbourg application was lodged on 28 April 2009.

case_name: CASE OF BOULOIS v. LUXEMBOURG
summary:
The applicant, Thomas Boulois, a French national born in 1972, was detained at Schrassig Prison in Luxembourg. On 15 December 1998 he was remanded in custody. By judgment of 22 October 2001, the Criminal Division of the Court of Appeal sentenced him to fifteen years’ imprisonment, three years suspended, for assault occasioning actual bodily harm, rape and false imprisonment accompanied by acts of torture committed on 10 December 1998. His divorce became final on 19 October 2000, and between 14 June 2001 and 13 April 2005 domestic court decisions concerned visiting rights in respect of his three minor children. The applicant alleged that he had been deprived of a fair hearing and access to a court in connection with decisions refusing his prison-leave requests.

While imprisoned, he made requests for conditional release, transfer to Givenich semi-open prison and prison leave. In October 2003 he submitted his first prison-leave request to the Attorney-General, seeking one day’s leave to complete administrative tasks, meet friends and deal with personal matters. He said he had not yet paid civil damages because of debts. Two psychologists certified in October and November 2003 that he had undertaken psychotherapy and wished to understand his offences and avoid reoffending. On 5 November 2003 the Prison Board refused the request through the Attorney-General’s representative, citing a risk of deportation because an application to the Ministry of Justice of 25 June 2003 remained undecided, a risk of absconding, lack of reflection on his crime, and the need to begin paying the civil party. On 17 January 2004 he made a second request on the same grounds; his lawyer argued it would aid rehabilitation and repayment. On 17 March 2004 the Attorney-General’s representative confirmed that the 5 November refusal remained valid.

On 25 May 2004 the applicant applied to the Administrative Court for judicial review of the 5 November 2003 and 17 March 2004 decisions. On 6 December 2004 the Administrative Court raised jurisdiction of its own motion; the Government left the issue to the court, while the applicant argued the court had jurisdiction. On 23 December 2004 the Administrative Court declined jurisdiction, distinguishing prison-treatment measures from decisions altering the nature or scope of a sentence; it held that granting or refusing prison leave altered the scope of the sentence and was judicial, not administrative. On 14 April 2005 the Higher Administrative Court upheld that ruling, finding that the request concerned execution of the sentence and was judicial in nature; the “scope” meant the manner of execution. It rejected the applicant’s arguments that no other remedy existed and that he had suffered a denial of justice.

Further prison-leave requests followed. On 11 August 2004 he requested leave to attend courses; on 21 September 2004 this was refused because he could attend courses in prison and had made no substantial compensation efforts. On 14 October 2004 he sought leave for St Nicholas with his children; on 14 December 2004 this was refused because visiting rights were not clearly established. On 24 February 2005 he requested leave for courses, identity papers, driving licence and debt repayment; on 23 March 2005 it was refused for failure to give reasons. On 12 July 2005 a sixth request was refused for risk of not returning. On 4 May 2006 a seventh was refused for lack of effort, especially regarding compensation, and refusal to abide by conditions.

After May 2006, the applicant wrote five times to the Attorney-General’s Department about repayment and reintegration conditions; on 6 November 2006 he was told no reply was intended. The Attorney-General later agreed to an interview on 20 November 2006, but the applicant says it never took place. Later, on 31 October 2008 he received one day’s leave; between 12 December 2008 and 19 June 2009 he received five two-day leaves; on 20 March 2009 he was transferred to Givenich semi-open prison and granted ten days’ leave for work and administrative tasks; on 24 June 2009 he signed a vocational rehabilitation contract as a cook; on 25 September 2009 conditional release was granted. Requests to suspend his sentence were refused on 25 September and 11 December 2009 and 26 February 2010. On 15 July 2010 his sentence was suspended and he left Givenich.

Under domestic law, the 1986 Law included prison leave among sentence-execution measures; leave could be granted for family, rehabilitation or reintegration reasons or as a trial for conditional release. Consideration was given to personality, progress and risk of reoffending. For sentences over two years, such measures were taken by the Attorney-General or representative in accordance with a majority decision of a board including a judge and a public prosecutor.

case_name: CASE OF ROHLENA v. THE CZECH REPUBLIC
summary:
Petr Rohlena, a Czech national born in 1966 living in Brno, lodged application no. 59552/08 against the Czech Republic on 4 December 2008. Relying on Article 7, he alleged that, in convicting him of a continuous criminal offence, the domestic courts had applied criminal law retroactively to his detriment.

On 29 May 2006, the Brno municipal prosecutor indicted him for repeatedly abusing his wife physically and mentally while drunk, at least between 2000 and 8 February 2006. He was accused of verbal abuse, hitting her head with his hand and fist, slapping her, holding her by the throat, trying to strangle her, throwing her against furniture or onto the ground, pushing her down stairs, and kicking her. He was also accused of hitting the children, gambling away household money, and smashing crockery. His wife sustained haematomas, bruising, and a fractured nose, and sought medical assistance on 26 June 2000, 18 July 2003, and 8 February 2006, following assaults on 24 June 2000, 17 July 2003, and 8 February 2006. The prosecutor alleged a continuing offence of abusing a person living under the same roof under Article 215a §§ 1 and 2(b) of the Criminal Code, because conduct before that offence was introduced on 1 June 2004 amounted to violence against an individual under Article 197a and assault occasioning bodily harm under Article 221.

On 18 April 2007, the Brno Municipal Court found him guilty as charged for conduct at least between 2000 and 8 February 2006. It sentenced him to a suspended term of two and a half years’ imprisonment, five years’ probation, supervision, and alcohol-dependency treatment. Evidence included statements from the applicant, his wife, witnesses, and the couple’s children, who reported ten verbal insults, four incidents of grabbing and strangling, and monthly verbal or physical assaults. The applicant admitted quarrels and physical violence, including slapping and hitting with his fist. The court applied Article 215a as in force since 1 June 2004, extending it to earlier acts because they had been punishable at the time at least under Article 197a. It found a relatively high degree of danger due to the duration, considered the two-to-eight-year range under Article 215a § 2, but imposed a lower suspended sentence due to extenuating circumstances.

On 6 September 2007, the Brno Regional Court dismissed the applicant’s appeal contesting the established facts and evidence. It found no defects and held that the classification conformed to the Criminal Code. On 21 February 2008, the Supreme Court dismissed his appeal on points of law, in which he complained that Article 215a had been applied to conduct before 1 June 2004. The Supreme Court held that a continuation of a criminal offence constituted a single act, classified under the law in force when the last occurrence was completed; earlier acts were punishable at least under Article 197a or Article 221 § 1; and his conduct disclosed the elements of Article 215a §§ 1 and 2(b), since abuse required duration and several years satisfied that element.

case_name: CASE OF VINTER AND OTHERS v. THE UNITED KINGDOM
summary:
The case concerns three British nationals, Douglas Gary Vinter, Jeremy Neville Bamber and Peter Howard Moore, each serving mandatory life imprisonment for murder in England and Wales and subject to whole life orders. They lodged applications against the United Kingdom on 11 December 2009, 17 December 2009 and 6 January 2010, alleging that the whole life orders amounted to ill-treatment contrary to Article 3 of the Convention.

Under the domestic regime, murder carries a mandatory life sentence. The trial judge sets a minimum term; exceptionally, a whole life order may be made where the offence’s seriousness is exceptionally high. A whole life prisoner cannot be released except at the Secretary of State’s discretion on compassionate grounds, generally where terminally ill or seriously incapacitated. For pre-2003 Act cases, tariffs or whole life tariffs were set by the Secretary of State; transitional provisions allowed the High Court to review and either set a minimum term or make a whole life order.

Vinter, born in 1969, received life imprisonment on 20 May 1996 for murdering a work colleague, with a ten-year minimum. He was released on licence on 4 August 2005. In February 2008 he killed his wife; he pleaded guilty to murder on 21 April 2008. The trial judge imposed a whole life order. The Court of Appeal dismissed his appeal on 25 June 2009, finding that a whole life order was appropriate because he was already a convicted murderer.

Bamber, born in 1961, was convicted on 28 October 1986 of murdering his parents, adoptive sister and her two children, who were shot and killed on 7 August 1985. The prosecution alleged premeditation, financial gain and staging of the scene. The trial judge recommended a minimum of twenty-five years; the Lord Chief Justice commented that he would never release him. In 1988 the Secretary of State imposed a whole life tariff; Bamber was informed on 15 December 1994. In 2008 the High Court reviewed the tariff and imposed a whole life order. The Court of Appeal dismissed his appeal on 14 May 2009. His application to certify a point of law for the House of Lords was refused on 23 June 2009.

Moore, born in 1946, was convicted on 29 November 1996 of four murders of homosexual men, each stabbed repeatedly with a combat knife. The attacks occurred on 23 September 1995, around 7 October 1995, 30 November 1995 and shortly before Christmas 1995. The trial judge recommended that he never be released; the Lord Chief Justice suggested thirty years. On 27 September 2002 the Secretary of State set a whole life tariff. In 2008 the High Court rejected the thirty-year recommendation and made a whole life order. The Court of Appeal dismissed his appeal on 26 February 2009. He was told on 14 August 2009 that he could not apply to certify a point of law for the House of Lords because permission to appeal had been refused.

case_name: CASE OF TSYOGE FON MANTEYFEL v. UKRAINE
summary:
Ms Karina Volodymyrivna Tsyoge fon Manteyfel, a Russian national born in 1978 living in Elektrostal, lodged application no. 29804/16 against Ukraine on 19 May 2016. She was represented by lawyers V. Lebid and M. Tarakhkalo, practising in Kyiv. The application concerns her compulsory psychiatric treatment. She suffers from paranoid schizophrenia and was subject to a court-ordered compulsory medical measure in criminal proceedings in which she had been charged with murder.

From 23 August 2010 to 14 November 2017 the applicant was detained in various psychiatric hospitals under different supervision regimes. During that period the domestic courts periodically reviewed her detention on the basis of submissions from the hospitals and extended her compulsory inpatient treatment. The most recent order for continued compulsory inpatient treatment was issued by the Samarskyy District Court of Dnipropetrovsk on 19 August 2016. According to the applicant, that order expired on 19 February 2017 because the Psychiatric Assistance Act required reviews of such orders at least every six months.

The Dnipro Psychiatric Hospital submitted requests on 13 January and 19 May 2017 for the applicant to continue compulsory inpatient treatment. Those requests were dismissed by the court on 13 May and 2 November 2017 respectively, and the court ordered that she be treated as an outpatient. The applicant was discharged from hospital on 14 November 2017.

The domestic courts did not examine the applicant’s subsequent appeals against the courts’ orders or her requests for release. Under the relevant law at the time, she did not have locus standi to lodge an appeal or initiate a review of the lawfulness of her continued detention. After 19 February 2017, requests for her immediate release lodged by her mother and her lawyer were dismissed by the hospital on the ground that there had been no court decision ordering her release.

In August 2017 the applicant brought a civil claim against the hospital. By a final domestic judgment of 19 June 2019, the Supreme Court partly allowed that claim. It declared that her continued detention after 19 February 2017—after expiry of the six-month period from the 19 August 2016 court decision and in the absence of any further decision extending her detention—had no basis in law. The Supreme Court noted in particular that the Psychiatric Assistance Act’s provision that extension of a compulsory medical measure was to be carried out each time for a period not exceeding six months was a guarantee against unlawful detention. The Supreme Court ordered the Dnipropetrovsk Court of Appeal to rule on the amount of compensation to be awarded to the applicant.

In January 2021 the Dnipropetrovsk Court of Appeal awarded the applicant 30,000 Ukrainian hryvnias for non-pecuniary damage. That judgment was not appealed by the parties and became final. The award remains unpaid to the applicant.

case_name: CASE OF PAPOSHVILI v. BELGIUM
summary:
The applicant, Georgie Paposhvili, a Georgian national born in 1958, arrived in Belgium via Italy on 25 November 1998 with his wife and a child. They applied for asylum the next day. Under the Dublin Convention, Germany refused a take-back request and Italy accepted responsibility on 4 June 1999. The asylum application was refused on 11 June 1999, and a further application lodged on 22 September 1999 under a false identity was rejected. Between 1998 and 2005 the applicant was convicted of theft, robbery and related offences; in 2005 the Ghent Court of Appeal sentenced him to three years’ imprisonment for involvement in a criminal organisation. He was held in several prisons and later in the Merksplas closed facility for illegal aliens.

In 2006 he was diagnosed with chronic lymphocytic leukaemia (Binet stage B). He received chemotherapy in 2007; an Antwerp University Hospital report of 11 February 2008 described his condition as life-threatening and estimated life expectancy at three to five years. By 2011 his leukaemia had progressed to Binet stage C. He also suffered from tuberculosis, COPD, hepatitis C and, after a 2015 stroke, permanent paralysis of the left arm. From December 2014 he received Ibrutinib. Medical reports in 2015 stated that discontinuing treatment would result in death, that he needed specialised haematology care and a donor stem cell transplant, and that such treatment would not be available in Georgia. Belgian medical advisers considered his condition serious but did not find a direct threat to life or a critical state.

The applicant made several regularisation requests. A first request on exceptional grounds (20 March 2000) was declared devoid of purpose and unfounded on 30 March 2004. A second request (28 April 2004) was declared inadmissible on 5 April 2007; the Aliens Appeals Board rejected his set-aside application on 29 February 2008. A third request on exceptional grounds was refused on 7 July 2010, when the Aliens Office also issued an order to leave the country and a detention order, served on 11 July 2010. His wife and three children were granted indefinite leave to remain on 29 July 2010. A stay/set-aside application concerning the 7 July 2010 decision and order was rejected by the Aliens Appeals Board on 16 March 2015 because the applicant did not attend or appoint representation.

On medical grounds, a first request on 10 September 2007 was refused on 26 September 2007 because he was excluded as having committed serious crimes, following a ministerial deportation order of 16 August 2007. The Aliens Appeals Board dismissed his challenge on 20 August 2008, noting that no removal measure accompanied the decision. A second medical request of 3 April 2008 was refused on 4 June 2008; the Aliens Appeals Board rejected his set-aside application on 21 May 2015, and the Conseil d’État declared his appeal on points of law inadmissible on 9 July 2015.

Removal measures included an order to leave under the Dublin Convention of 10 June 1999, the ministerial deportation order of 16 August 2007 imposing a ten-year re-entry ban, the 7 July 2010 order to leave and detention, and an order to leave with immediate effect of 18 February 2012. The applicant was transferred to Merksplas in July 2010, and a Georgian travel document was issued on 16 July 2010. On 28 July 2010 the European Court of Human Rights requested Belgium not to remove him pending the Aliens Appeals Board proceedings; he was released on 30 July 2010. On 23 July 2010 he had applied to the Court alleging that removal to Georgia would risk his life and physical well-being and violate his family life under Articles 2, 3 and 8. He died on 7 June 2016; on 20 June 2016 his wife and three children expressed the wish to pursue the proceedings. The Georgian Government intervened.

case_name: CASE OF SHIPS WASTE OIL COLLECTOR B.V. AND OTHERS v. THE NETHERLANDS
summary:
Six Dutch limited-liability companies in two groups complained that intercept data lawfully obtained in criminal investigations had been transmitted to competition authorities and used against them, violating Article 8, and that they lacked an effective domestic remedy under Articles 8 and 13. The first group (Ships Waste Oil Collector B.V., Burando Holding B.V., Port Invest B.V.) collected waste liquids in Rotterdam. The second (Janssen de Jong Groep B.V., Janssen de Jong Infrastructuur Nederland B.V., Janssen de Jong Infra B.V.) operated in construction.

First group: In late 2006 the VROM-IOD began criminal investigation “Toto” into the I. company for suspected forgery and environmental offences. An investigating judge authorised interception of telephone calls by I. employees, including calls with Ships Waste Oil Collector employees; some suggested price-fixing. On 21 October 2008 the public prosecutor approved transmission to the Netherlands Competition Authority (NMA) of a 21 April 2008 official record and transcripts; transmission occurred on 29 June 2009. Further transcripts and recordings were authorised on 23 October 2009. NMA inspectors visited premises on 29–30 June 2010 and questioned managers, playing an intercepted recording. More data were sent in 2010 after approvals in June, July and August; the last transmission was 8–9 September 2010. In the criminal case, the I. company and an employee settled on 11 March 2010 for EUR 50,000 and EUR 4,000; on 5 July 2010 the Rotterdam Regional Court declared the prosecution inadmissible. The NMA’s 28 December 2010 report found collusion from 30 August 2005 to 31 July 2007 contrary to section 6 of the Competition Act. On 16 November 2011 it fined Ships Waste Oil Collector EUR 834,000 and the other three jointly and severally EUR 1,861,000, with Burando’s liability capped at EUR 621,000.

The companies objected that the intercepts were not transmissible “criminal data,” that there was no prior judicial review, that Ships Waste Oil Collector was never suspected, that the settlement prevented ex post facto judicial review, that the NMA lacked intercept powers, and that prior contacts lacked a legal basis. On 11 July 2013 the Rotterdam Regional Court held the data were criminal data but excluded them because the prosecutor’s approvals lacked an identifiable weighing of interests; it quashed the NMA decisions. On 9 July 2015 the Supreme Administrative Court for Trade and Industry quashed that judgment, finding the data qualified as criminal data, a compelling general interest existed, written reasoning was not required, and the transmissions did not breach Article 8. It held the criminal case ended when the 5 July 2010 ruling became final on 19 July 2010. On 20 October 2016 the Regional Court found infringement from 1 January 2006 to 31 July 2007 and reduced fines; on 30 October 2018 the Supreme Administrative Court restored the original fines.

Second group: Around 2007 the “Cleveland” investigation by the Public Prosecution Service and Rijksrecherche examined suspected bribery of local officials; the Janssen companies were suspects. Interceptions were authorised for bribery, fraud and forgery. In July 2008 police gave NMA officials confidential access to transcripts; on 19 August 2008 the prosecutor provided a CD of about thirty recordings for information only. On 9 December 2008 the NMA opened a Competition Act investigation; on 16 December 2008 the prosecutor permitted use of the Cleveland information. Transcripts were transmitted on 24 December 2008. In civil proceedings, the provisional-measures judge on 26 June 2009 dismissed the Janssen companies’ claims, finding the data were criminal data and the transmission compatible with Article 8. NMA reports of 17 December 2009 and 25 February 2010 found infringement; on 29 October 2010 it imposed a EUR 3,000,000 joint fine. The objection was dismissed on 8 March 2012. On 13 June 2013 the Rotterdam Regional Court quashed the decision because no identifiable weighing of interests by the prosecutor existed, although the data were criminal data.

case_name: CASE OF CENTRUM FÖR RÄTTVISA v. SWEDEN
summary:
The applicant, Centrum för rättvisa, is a Swedish foundation established in 2002 and based in Stockholm. It represents clients in proceedings concerning Convention rights, undertakes education and research, and participates in public debate on individual rights. It communicates daily by email, telephone and fax with individuals, organisations and companies in Sweden and abroad. It asserts that much of this communication is privacy-sensitive and that, because it scrutinises State actors, there is a risk that its communications have been or will be intercepted and examined through signals intelligence. On 14 July 2008 it lodged an application against Sweden, alleging that Swedish legislation and practice in the field of signals intelligence violated its rights under Article 8 and that it lacked an effective remedy contrary to Article 13. It did not bring any domestic proceedings, contending that no effective remedy existed for its complaints.

Domestically, foreign intelligence is regulated by the Foreign Intelligence Act (2000:130) and signals intelligence by the Signals Intelligence Act (2008:717), which entered into force on 1 January 2009 and was amended in 2009, 2013, 2015 and 2016. The National Defence Radio Establishment (FRA) is authorised to conduct signals intelligence. Signals intelligence involves intercepting, processing, analysing and reporting intelligence from electronic signals, including content and communications data, over airways and cables. Most relevant traffic is cable-based. Cable-based cross-border communications are transferred to collection points, from which limited data traffic is transferred to the FRA. Communications between a sender and receiver both within Sweden may not be intercepted; if they cannot be separated, recordings or notes must be destroyed once their domestic nature becomes clear.

The FRA may conduct signals intelligence only under detailed tasking directives issued by certain authorities, and it may not solely target a specific natural person. Permitted purposes include external military threats, international peacekeeping threats, strategic international terrorism or serious cross-border crime, weapons of mass destruction, threats to societal infrastructure, foreign conflicts, foreign intelligence operations against Swedish interests, and certain actions of foreign powers. The FRA also conducts “development activities”. Interception of cable-based signals is automated and uses selectors; selectors directly relating to a specific natural person may be used only if exceptionally important. Permits are issued by the Foreign Intelligence Court, subject to conditions, for maximum six months, renewable. In urgent cases the FRA may grant a permit itself, subject to immediate court review. The court may sit behind closed doors, with a privacy protection representative present.

Intercepted data must be destroyed in certain cases, including data concerning a specific person lacking importance, protected anonymous authorship or media sources, attorney-client privilege, or religious confession. The FRA Personal Data Processing Act and related ordinances regulate personal data, sensitive data, storage, destruction and communication to other authorities or foreign States. Supervision is carried out by the Foreign Intelligence Inspectorate, which conducted 102 inspections from 2009 to 2017, issuing 15 opinions to the FRA and one to the Government; no inspection led to a decision to cease collection or destroy results. Other oversight includes the Privacy Protection Council, data protection officers, the Data Protection Authority, Parliamentary Ombudsmen and the Chancellor of Justice.

Notification of secret surveillance is required if selectors directly related to a specific person were used, but may be delayed for secrecy and need not be given after one year or where measures concern a foreign power. Individuals may ask the Inspectorate to investigate whether their communications were intercepted; 132 requests were handled from 2010 to 2017, with no unlawfulness established. Other remedies include requests to the FRA for information or correction, appeals to the Administrative Court, and damages claims via the Chancellor of Justice. A 2010 Data Protection Authority report was overall positive but noted that notification had never been used due to secrecy considerations.

case_name: CASE OF AL-DULIMI AND MONTANA MANAGEMENT INC. v. SWITZERLAND
summary:
The first applicant, Khalaf M. Al-Dulimi, born in 1941, is an Iraqi national living in Amman, Jordan. According to the UN Security Council, he was head of finance for the Iraqi secret services under Saddam Hussein. The second applicant, Montana Management Inc., is a company incorporated under Panamanian law with its registered office in Panama; the first applicant was its managing director. The applicants alleged that Swiss authorities confiscated their assets pursuant to a UN Security Council resolution without any procedure complying with Article 6 of the Convention.

After Iraq invaded Kuwait on 2 August 1990, the UN Security Council adopted Resolutions 661 (1990) and 670 (1990), imposing an embargo. On 7 August 1990 the Swiss Federal Council adopted the Iraq Ordinance providing for economic measures against Iraq. The applicants alleged that their Swiss assets had been frozen since that date. Switzerland became a UN member on 10 September 2002.

On 22 May 2003, UN Security Council Resolution 1483 (2003) superseded Resolution 661 (1990), among others. It required states to freeze and transfer to the Development Fund for Iraq funds of the former Iraqi Government, Saddam Hussein, senior officials of the former regime, their immediate family members, and entities owned or controlled by them. The Iraq Ordinance was amended, notably on 30 October 2002 and 28 May 2003. On 24 November 2003, a sanctions committee created by Resolution 1518 (2003) was tasked with listing the individuals and entities concerned. On 26 April 2004, that committee added the second applicant and the first applicant to its list. On 12 May 2004, their names were added to the national list under Article 2 of the Iraq Ordinance. On 18 May 2004, the Federal Council adopted the Confiscation Ordinance on confiscation of frozen Iraqi assets and transfer to the Development Fund for Iraq; it was initially valid until 30 June 2010 and later extended to 30 June 2013.

The first applicant sought removal from the 1518 Sanctions Committee’s list. On 25 August 2004 he asked the Federal Department for Economic Affairs to suspend the confiscation procedure. On 5 November 2004 the Swiss government supported his application to the Committee. On 3 December 2004 the Committee Chair said the application was under consideration and requested supporting documents. On 21 January 2005 the first applicant asked to give oral evidence; no action followed. On 1 September 2005 the applicants sought continuation of the Swiss confiscation procedure. On 22 May 2006 the Federal Department sent a draft confiscation decision, which the applicants challenged on 22 June 2006.

On 16 November 2006, the Federal Department for Economic Affairs ordered confiscation of CHF 86,276.85 belonging to the first applicant and CHF 164,731,213 and CHF 104,739,882.57 held in the second applicant’s name at two banks, to be transferred within ninety days to the Development Fund for Iraq. It relied on the Sanctions Committee lists and stated that Switzerland could not delete a name unless the Committee did so. It noted that an administrative-law appeal could be lodged with the Federal Court.

On 19 December 2006, Resolution 1730 (2006) created a delisting procedure. The applicants appealed to the Federal Court against the three confiscation decisions, arguing that the confiscation breached property rights and that the listing procedure violated procedural safeguards under Article 14 ICCPR, Articles 6 and 13 of the Convention, and the Federal Constitution. They argued that Swiss authorities could review the conformity of the listing with those instruments. On 23 January 2008, the Federal Court dismissed the appeals in three almost identical judgments, confining itself to verifying that the applicants’ names appeared on the Sanctions Committee lists and that the assets belonged to them. It granted a brief final period before implementation to allow a new delisting application under Resolution 1730.

After the application was lodged, a delisting application under Resolution 1730 was rejected on 6 January 2009. SECO authorised releases from frozen funds for lawyers’ fees and court costs, amounting to approximately CHF 850,000 and over CHF 200,000 respectively. On 6 March 2009 the Swiss authorities stayed execution of the confiscation decisions pending the European Court proceedings. On 20 December 2013 further confiscation decisions were issued concerning assets in the first applicant’s name in two banks, to be transferred to successor funds if the application was rejected or the 2006 decisions were confirmed on review; the Federal Administrative Court suspended related proceedings on 7 May 2014.

case_name: CASE OF BOULOIS v. LUXEMBOURG
summary:
The applicant, Thomas Boulois, a French national born in 1972, was detained at Schrassig Prison in Luxembourg. On 15 December 1998 he was remanded in custody. By judgment of 22 October 2001, the Criminal Division of the Court of Appeal sentenced him to fifteen years’ imprisonment, three years suspended, for assault occasioning actual bodily harm, rape and false imprisonment accompanied by acts of torture committed on 10 December 1998. His divorce became final on 19 October 2000, and between 14 June 2001 and 13 April 2005 domestic court decisions concerned visiting rights in respect of his three minor children. The applicant alleged that he had been deprived of a fair hearing and access to a court in connection with decisions refusing his prison-leave requests.

While imprisoned, he made requests for conditional release, transfer to Givenich semi-open prison and prison leave. In October 2003 he submitted his first prison-leave request to the Attorney-General, seeking one day’s leave to complete administrative tasks, meet friends and deal with personal matters. He said he had not yet paid civil damages because of debts. Two psychologists certified in October and November 2003 that he had undertaken psychotherapy and wished to understand his offences and avoid reoffending. On 5 November 2003 the Prison Board refused the request through the Attorney-General’s representative, citing a risk of deportation because an application to the Ministry of Justice of 25 June 2003 remained undecided, a risk of absconding, lack of reflection on his crime, and the need to begin paying the civil party. On 17 January 2004 he made a second request on the same grounds; his lawyer argued it would aid rehabilitation and repayment. On 17 March 2004 the Attorney-General’s representative confirmed that the 5 November refusal remained valid.

On 25 May 2004 the applicant applied to the Administrative Court for judicial review of the 5 November 2003 and 17 March 2004 decisions. On 6 December 2004 the Administrative Court raised jurisdiction of its own motion; the Government left the issue to the court, while the applicant argued the court had jurisdiction. On 23 December 2004 the Administrative Court declined jurisdiction, distinguishing prison-treatment measures from decisions altering the nature or scope of a sentence; it held that granting or refusing prison leave altered the scope of the sentence and was judicial, not administrative. On 14 April 2005 the Higher Administrative Court upheld that ruling, finding that the request concerned execution of the sentence and was judicial in nature; the “scope” meant the manner of execution. It rejected the applicant’s arguments that no other remedy existed and that he had suffered a denial of justice.

Further prison-leave requests followed. On 11 August 2004 he requested leave to attend courses; on 21 September 2004 this was refused because he could attend courses in prison and had made no substantial compensation efforts. On 14 October 2004 he sought leave for St Nicholas with his children; on 14 December 2004 this was refused because visiting rights were not clearly established. On 24 February 2005 he requested leave for courses, identity papers, driving licence and debt repayment; on 23 March 2005 it was refused for failure to give reasons. On 12 July 2005 a sixth request was refused for risk of not returning. On 4 May 2006 a seventh was refused for lack of effort, especially regarding compensation, and refusal to abide by conditions.

After May 2006, the applicant wrote five times to the Attorney-General’s Department about repayment and reintegration conditions; on 6 November 2006 he was told no reply was intended. The Attorney-General later agreed to an interview on 20 November 2006, but the applicant says it never took place. Later, on 31 October 2008 he received one day’s leave; between 12 December 2008 and 19 June 2009 he received five two-day leaves; on 20 March 2009 he was transferred to Givenich semi-open prison and granted ten days’ leave for work and administrative tasks; on 24 June 2009 he signed a vocational rehabilitation contract as a cook; on 25 September 2009 conditional release was granted. Requests to suspend his sentence were refused on 25 September and 11 December 2009 and 26 February 2010. On 15 July 2010 his sentence was suspended and he left Givenich.

Under domestic law, the 1986 Law included prison leave among sentence-execution measures; leave could be granted for family, rehabilitation or reintegration reasons or as a trial for conditional release. Consideration was given to personality, progress and risk of reoffending. For sentences over two years, such measures were taken by the Attorney-General or representative in accordance with a majority decision of a board including a judge and a public prosecutor.

case_name: CASE OF VINTER AND OTHERS v. THE UNITED KINGDOM
summary:
The case concerns three British nationals, Douglas Gary Vinter, Jeremy Neville Bamber and Peter Howard Moore, each serving mandatory life imprisonment for murder in England and Wales and subject to whole life orders. They lodged applications against the United Kingdom on 11 December 2009, 17 December 2009 and 6 January 2010, alleging that the whole life orders amounted to ill-treatment contrary to Article 3 of the Convention.

Under the domestic regime, murder carries a mandatory life sentence. The trial judge sets a minimum term; exceptionally, a whole life order may be made where the offence’s seriousness is exceptionally high. A whole life prisoner cannot be released except at the Secretary of State’s discretion on compassionate grounds, generally where terminally ill or seriously incapacitated. For pre-2003 Act cases, tariffs or whole life tariffs were set by the Secretary of State; transitional provisions allowed the High Court to review and either set a minimum term or make a whole life order.

Vinter, born in 1969, received life imprisonment on 20 May 1996 for murdering a work colleague, with a ten-year minimum. He was released on licence on 4 August 2005. In February 2008 he killed his wife; he pleaded guilty to murder on 21 April 2008. The trial judge imposed a whole life order. The Court of Appeal dismissed his appeal on 25 June 2009, finding that a whole life order was appropriate because he was already a convicted murderer.

Bamber, born in 1961, was convicted on 28 October 1986 of murdering his parents, adoptive sister and her two children, who were shot and killed on 7 August 1985. The prosecution alleged premeditation, financial gain and staging of the scene. The trial judge recommended a minimum of twenty-five years; the Lord Chief Justice commented that he would never release him. In 1988 the Secretary of State imposed a whole life tariff; Bamber was informed on 15 December 1994. In 2008 the High Court reviewed the tariff and imposed a whole life order. The Court of Appeal dismissed his appeal on 14 May 2009. His application to certify a point of law for the House of Lords was refused on 23 June 2009.

Moore, born in 1946, was convicted on 29 November 1996 of four murders of homosexual men, each stabbed repeatedly with a combat knife. The attacks occurred on 23 September 1995, around 7 October 1995, 30 November 1995 and shortly before Christmas 1995. The trial judge recommended that he never be released; the Lord Chief Justice suggested thirty years. On 27 September 2002 the Secretary of State set a whole life tariff. In 2008 the High Court rejected the thirty-year recommendation and made a whole life order. The Court of Appeal dismissed his appeal on 26 February 2009. He was told on 14 August 2009 that he could not apply to certify a point of law for the House of Lords because permission to appeal had been refused.

case_name: CASE OF FERNÁNDEZ MARTÍNEZ v. SPAIN
summary:
José Antonio Fernández Martínez, a Spanish national born in 1937 and living in Cieza, was ordained a Catholic priest in 1961. case_name: CASE OF ROHLENA v. THE CZECH REPUBLIC
summary:
Petr Rohlena, a Czech national born in 1966 living in Brno, lodged application no. 59552/08 against the Czech Republic on 4 December 2008. Relying on Article 7, he alleged that, in convicting him of a continuous criminal offence, the domestic courts had applied criminal law retroactively to his detriment.

On 29 May 2006, the Brno municipal prosecutor indicted him for repeatedly abusing his wife physically and mentally while drunk, at least between 2000 and 8 February 2006. He was accused of verbal abuse, hitting her head with his hand and fist, slapping her, holding her by the throat, trying to strangle her, throwing her against furniture or onto the ground, pushing her down stairs, and kicking her. He was also accused of hitting the children, gambling away household money, and smashing crockery. His wife sustained haematomas, bruising, and a fractured nose, and sought medical assistance on 26 June 2000, 18 July 2003, and 8 February 2006, following assaults on 24 June 2000, 17 July 2003, and 8 February 2006. The prosecutor alleged a continuing offence of abusing a person living under the same roof under Article 215a §§ 1 and 2(b) of the Criminal Code, because conduct before that offence was introduced on 1 June 2004 amounted to violence against an individual under Article 197a and assault occasioning bodily harm under Article 221.

On 18 April 2007, the Brno Municipal Court found him guilty as charged for conduct at least between 2000 and 8 February 2006. It sentenced him to a suspended term of two and a half years’ imprisonment, five years’ probation, supervision, and alcohol-dependency treatment. Evidence included statements from the applicant, his wife, witnesses, and the couple’s children, who reported ten verbal insults, four incidents of grabbing and strangling, and monthly verbal or physical assaults. The applicant admitted quarrels and physical violence, including slapping and hitting with his fist. The court applied Article 215a as in force since 1 June 2004, extending it to earlier acts because they had been punishable at the time at least under Article 197a. It found a relatively high degree of danger due to the duration, considered the two-to-eight-year range under Article 215a § 2, but imposed a lower suspended sentence due to extenuating circumstances.

On 6 September 2007, the Brno Regional Court dismissed the applicant’s appeal contesting the established facts and evidence. It found no defects and held that the classification conformed to the Criminal Code. On 21 February 2008, the Supreme Court dismissed his appeal on points of law, in which he complained that Article 215a had been applied to conduct before 1 June 2004. The Supreme Court held that a continuation of a criminal offence constituted a single act, classified under the law in force when the last occurrence was completed; earlier acts were punishable at least under Article 197a or Article 221 § 1; and his conduct disclosed the elements of Article 215a §§ 1 and 2(b), since abuse required duration and several years satisfied that element.

On 10 June 2008, the Constitutional Court dismissed his constitutional appeal alleging unfair proceedings and retroactive detriment. It held that the domestic decisions were logical and coherent and had no prohibited retroactive effect.

Relevant domestic law provided that criminality was assessed under the law in force at the time of the act, with a more favourable later law applied. Article 89 § 3 defined a continuation of an offence as individual acts driven by the same purpose, comprising the same offence, similarly executed, close in time, and pursuing the same object. Article 215a, introduced on 1 June 2004, punished abuse of a relative or cohabitant by up to three years, or two to eight years if continued over a lengthy period. Article 197a punished threats by up to one year or a fine; Article 221 § 1 punished assault with intent to cause bodily harm by up to two years.

Later, because the applicant committed another offence while on probation and did not undergo alcohol treatment, he was required to serve the prison sentence. He began serving it on 3 January 2011. According to the Government, he was conditionally released on 17 May 2012.

case_name: CASE OF BOUYID v. BELGIUM
summary:
The applicants, Saïd and Mohamed Bouyid, Belgian nationals born in 1986 and 1979 respectively, are brothers living with their family in Saint-Josse-ten-Noode, next to the local police station. They alleged that they were each slapped in the face by police officers at that station—one on 8 December 2003 and the other on 23 February 2004—against a background of tense relations between their family and certain officers. The Government disputed both allegations.

As to 8 December 2003, the applicants submitted that, at around 4 p.m., the first applicant was outside his building with a friend, ringing the bell because he had forgotten his keys. A plain-clothes officer, A.Z., asked to see his identity card. The first applicant refused and asked to see A.Z.’s credentials. A.Z. then grabbed him by his jacket, tearing it, and took him to the police station. There, while alone with A.Z. in a room, the officer allegedly slapped him in the face as he protested about his arrest. A medical certificate issued at 7.20 p.m. the same day stated that the first applicant was “in a state of shock” and noted “erythema on the left cheek (disappearing)” and “erythema on the left-side external auditory canal.” The Government submitted that, because the first applicant refused to show his identity card, A.Z. had no choice but to take him to the station for identification. It said the first applicant caused a scene, insulted an officer, and was released after identity checks; he was told a report would be filed for forceful resistance, abusive behaviour and verbal threats. He later returned with his parents accusing A.Z. of slapping him, which A.Z. denied. At 6 p.m. A.Z. lodged a criminal complaint against him.

As to 23 February 2004, the applicants submitted that between 9.44 a.m. and 10.20 a.m., while the second applicant was being interviewed by Officer P.P. at the station about an altercation involving him and his mother and a third party, P.P. asked him not to lean on his desk and then slapped him in the face. He allegedly forced him to sign his statement by threatening to place him in a cell. A medical certificate issued that day recorded “bruising [on the] left cheek”; it was presented to the Standing Committee for the oversight of police services (“Committee P”) before 11.20 a.m. The Government described the second applicant as arrogant during the interview—slouching, leaning on the desk, laughing, giving pithy answers—and said he changed his statement and threatened the officers on leaving. It stated that P.P. remained calm and patient, admitted grabbing the applicant by the arm to make him leave, but denied slapping him.

The first applicant complained to Committee P at 9.42 a.m. on 9 December 2003; the second complained at 11.20 a.m. on 23 February 2004. Their mother was also interviewed on 23 February 2004 and filed a complaint concerning P.P.’s attitude. On 5 May 2004, P.P. was interviewed by the internal oversight director and denied slapping the second applicant. On 17 June 2004, the applicants applied to intervene as civil parties in respect of harassment, arbitrary interference with fundamental freedoms, abuse of authority, arbitrary arrest and wounding with intent, expressly relying on the events of 8 December 2003 and 23 February 2004. Officers A.Z. and P.P. were charged with using violence against individuals in the course of their duties, intentional wounding or assault, and arbitrary acts. After a judicial investigation, the Crown Prosecutor sought discontinuance on 10 November 2005, and the Committals Division of the Brussels Court of First Instance discontinued the proceedings on 27 November 2007. On 9 April 2008, the Indictments Division of the Brussels Court of Appeal upheld the discontinuance, referring to inconsistent statements, lack of evidence, and a Committee P report on the family’s general conduct. The Court of Cassation dismissed an appeal on points of law on 29 October 2008. Separately, on 5 February 2008, six family members, including the applicants, filed a civil-party complaint about earlier facts; in a judgment of 30 May 2012, the Brussels Court of First Instance declared prosecution of those offences time-barred, and no appeal appears to have been lodged. The Strasbourg application was lodged on 28 April 2009.

case_name: CASE OF PENTIKÄINEN v. FINLAND
summary:
The applicant, Markus Veikko Pentikäinen, born in 1980 and living in Helsinki, is a photographer and journalist employed by the weekly magazine *Suomen Kuvalehti*. On 9 September 2006 he was sent by his employer to photograph the “Smash ASEM” demonstration in Helsinki, held in protest against the Asia-Europe Meeting. He was to report for the magazine’s print edition and publish online once the demonstration ended.

Before the event, Finnish Security Intelligence assessed the demonstration as hostile and without a clear political message. The police had difficulty contacting the organisers. Two earlier Helsinki demonstrations that year had turned violent. The announced march was to run from the Kiasma Museum to near the ASEM summit venue. Posters invited participants to wear black and referred to bringing “mayhem” to Helsinki’s streets.

The demonstration began at 6 p.m. About 500 bystanders, a core group of demonstrators, and some 50 journalists gathered. Violence soon broke out: bottles, stones, and paint-filled jars were thrown at police and the public. Police cordoned the area, announced that a peaceful demonstration was allowed but not a march, and later declared the event a riot. From 6.30 p.m. to 7.17 p.m. they sealed off the area. Police allowed families and media representatives to pass through, though projectiles were thrown at times. They repeatedly ordered the crowd to disperse. The applicant claimed he first heard the order around 8.30 p.m. and understood it as applying only to demonstrators. He called his employer and decided to stay. Around 9 p.m. a police officer told him personally he had one last chance to leave. The applicant said he was reporting for *Suomen Kuvalehti* and would follow the event to the end; the officer left him alone.

Later, police broke up remaining demonstrators and apprehended protesters. The applicant claimed he heard an officer shout, “Get the photographer!” He was taking photographs when apprehended. He told the officer he was a journalist and presented his press card; the officer later confirmed this. The applicant did not resist. The stated basis for apprehension was contumacy towards police. He was taken to a detention bus and then a police station, where he said he again identified himself as a journalist and wore his press card visibly. He claimed his camera equipment and memory cards were confiscated. The Government maintained that once police learned he was press, his equipment was treated as journalistic material and not confiscated; he retained the photographs. A Deputy Parliamentary Ombudsman report noted that police checked detainees’ mobile phones, though it was unclear whether the applicant’s phone or memory cards were inspected.

The applicant was detained from 9 September at 9.26 p.m. until 10 September at 3.05 p.m., about seventeen and a half hours. He was interrogated on 10 September between 1.32 p.m. and 1.57 p.m. Police apprehended 128 people in total; most were released on 11 September. The applicant was the seventh detainee interrogated and the sixth released after minors.

On 23 May 2007 the public prosecutor charged the applicant with contumacy towards the police under Chapter 16, section 4(1), of the Penal Code. On 17 December 2007 Helsinki District Court found him guilty but waived punishment under Chapter 6, section 12(3), treating the offence as comparable to an excusable act because of conflicting expectations from police and his profession. The court found police orders lawful, clear, and applicable to everyone, and concluded that restricting his freedom of expression was justified. The applicant appealed, arguing his apprehension and conviction violated the Constitution and Article 10. On 30 April 2009 the Court of Appeal dismissed the appeal without further reasons. On 1 September 2009 the Supreme Court refused leave to appeal.

The applicant alleged before the European Court that his Article 10 rights were violated because police ordered him to leave, he could not transmit information during his detention, and he was suspected, charged, and convicted, creating a chilling effect on his work.

case_name: CASE OF AL-DULIMI AND MONTANA MANAGEMENT INC. v. SWITZERLAND
summary:
The first applicant, Khalaf M. Al-Dulimi, born in 1941, is an Iraqi national living in Amman, Jordan. According to the UN Security Council, he was head of finance for the Iraqi secret services under Saddam Hussein. The second applicant, Montana Management Inc., is a company incorporated under Panamanian law with its registered office in Panama; the first applicant was its managing director. The applicants alleged that Swiss authorities confiscated their assets pursuant to a UN Security Council resolution without any procedure complying with Article 6 of the Convention.

After Iraq invaded Kuwait on 2 August 1990, the UN Security Council adopted Resolutions 661 (1990) and 670 (1990), imposing an embargo. On 7 August 1990 the Swiss Federal Council adopted the Iraq Ordinance providing for economic measures against Iraq. The applicants alleged that their Swiss assets had been frozen since that date. Switzerland became a UN member on 10 September 2002.

On 22 May 2003, UN Security Council Resolution 1483 (2003) superseded Resolution 661 (1990), among others. It required states to freeze and transfer to the Development Fund for Iraq funds of the former Iraqi Government, Saddam Hussein, senior officials of the former regime, their immediate family members, and entities owned or controlled by them. The Iraq Ordinance was amended, notably on 30 October 2002 and 28 May 2003. On 24 November 2003, a sanctions committee created by Resolution 1518 (2003) was tasked with listing the individuals and entities concerned. On 26 April 2004, that committee added the second applicant and the first applicant to its list. On 12 May 2004, their names were added to the national list under Article 2 of the Iraq Ordinance. On 18 May 2004, the Federal Council adopted the Confiscation Ordinance on confiscation of frozen Iraqi assets and transfer to the Development Fund for Iraq; it was initially valid until 30 June 2010 and later extended to 30 June 2013.

The first applicant sought removal from the 1518 Sanctions Committee’s list. On 25 August 2004 he asked the Federal Department for Economic Affairs to suspend the confiscation procedure. On 5 November 2004 the Swiss government supported his application to the Committee. On 3 December 2004 the Committee Chair said the application was under consideration and requested supporting documents. On 21 January 2005 the first applicant asked to give oral evidence; no action followed. On 1 September 2005 the applicants sought continuation of the Swiss confiscation procedure. On 22 May 2006 the Federal Department sent a draft confiscation decision, which the applicants challenged on 22 June 2006.

On 16 November 2006, the Federal Department for Economic Affairs ordered confiscation of CHF 86,276.85 belonging to the first applicant and CHF 164,731,213 and CHF 104,739,882.57 held in the second applicant’s name at two banks, to be transferred within ninety days to the Development Fund for Iraq. It relied on the Sanctions Committee lists and stated that Switzerland could not delete a name unless the Committee did so. It noted that an administrative-law appeal could be lodged with the Federal Court.

On 19 December 2006, Resolution 1730 (2006) created a delisting procedure. case_name: CASE OF PAPOSHVILI v. BELGIUM
summary:
The applicant, Georgie Paposhvili, a Georgian national born in 1958, arrived in Belgium via Italy on 25 November 1998 with his wife and a child. They applied for asylum the next day. Under the Dublin Convention, Germany refused a take-back request and Italy accepted responsibility on 4 June 1999. The asylum application was refused on 11 June 1999, and a further application lodged on 22 September 1999 under a false identity was rejected. Between 1998 and 2005 the applicant was convicted of theft, robbery and related offences; in 2005 the Ghent Court of Appeal sentenced him to three years’ imprisonment for involvement in a criminal organisation. He was held in several prisons and later in the Merksplas closed facility for illegal aliens.

In 2006 he was diagnosed with chronic lymphocytic leukaemia (Binet stage B). He received chemotherapy in 2007; an Antwerp University Hospital report of 11 February 2008 described his condition as life-threatening and estimated life expectancy at three to five years. By 2011 his leukaemia had progressed to Binet stage C. He also suffered from tuberculosis, COPD, hepatitis C and, after a 2015 stroke, permanent paralysis of the left arm. From December 2014 he received Ibrutinib. Medical reports in 2015 stated that discontinuing treatment would result in death, that he needed specialised haematology care and a donor stem cell transplant, and that such treatment would not be available in Georgia. Belgian medical advisers considered his condition serious but did not find a direct threat to life or a critical state.

The applicant made several regularisation requests. A first request on exceptional grounds (20 March 2000) was declared devoid of purpose and unfounded on 30 March 2004. A second request (28 April 2004) was declared inadmissible on 5 April 2007; the Aliens Appeals Board rejected his set-aside application on 29 February 2008. A third request on exceptional grounds was refused on 7 July 2010, when the Aliens Office also issued an order to leave the country and a detention order, served on 11 July 2010. His wife and three children were granted indefinite leave to remain on 29 July 2010. A stay/set-aside application concerning the 7 July 2010 decision and order was rejected by the Aliens Appeals Board on 16 March 2015 because the applicant did not attend or appoint representation.

On medical grounds, a first request on 10 September 2007 was refused on 26 September 2007 because he was excluded as having committed serious crimes, following a ministerial deportation order of 16 August 2007. The Aliens Appeals Board dismissed his challenge on 20 August 2008, noting that no removal measure accompanied the decision. A second medical request of 3 April 2008 was refused on 4 June 2008; the Aliens Appeals Board rejected his set-aside application on 21 May 2015, and the Conseil d’État declared his appeal on points of law inadmissible on 9 July 2015.

Removal measures included an order to leave under the Dublin Convention of 10 June 1999, the ministerial deportation order of 16 August 2007 imposing a ten-year re-entry ban, the 7 July 2010 order to leave and detention, and an order to leave with immediate effect of 18 February 2012. The applicant was transferred to Merksplas in July 2010, and a Georgian travel document was issued on 16 July 2010. On 28 July 2010 the European Court of Human Rights requested Belgium not to remove him pending the Aliens Appeals Board proceedings; he was released on 30 July 2010. On 23 July 2010 he had applied to the Court alleging that removal to Georgia would risk his life and physical well-being and violate his family life under Articles 2, 3 and 8. He died on 7 June 2016; on 20 June 2016 his wife and three children expressed the wish to pursue the proceedings. The Georgian Government intervened.

case_name: CASE OF CENTRUM FÖR RÄTTVISA v. SWEDEN
summary:
The applicant, Centrum för rättvisa, is a Swedish foundation established in 2002 and based in Stockholm. It represents clients in proceedings concerning Convention rights, undertakes education and research, and participates in public debate on individual rights. It communicates daily by email, telephone and fax with individuals, organisations and companies in Sweden and abroad. It asserts that much of this communication is privacy-sensitive and that, because it scrutinises State actors, there is a risk that its communications have been or will be intercepted and examined through signals intelligence. On 14 July 2008 it lodged an application against Sweden, alleging that Swedish legislation and practice in the field of signals intelligence violated its rights under Article 8 and that it lacked an effective remedy contrary to Article 13. It did not bring any domestic proceedings, contending that no effective remedy existed for its complaints.

Domestically, foreign intelligence is regulated by the Foreign Intelligence Act (2000:130) and signals intelligence by the Signals Intelligence Act (2008:717), which entered into force on 1 January 2009 and was amended in 2009, 2013, 2015 and 2016. The National Defence Radio Establishment (FRA) is authorised to conduct signals intelligence. Signals intelligence involves intercepting, processing, analysing and reporting intelligence from electronic signals, including content and communications data, over airways and cables. Most relevant traffic is cable-based. Cable-based cross-border communications are transferred to collection points, from which limited data traffic is transferred to the FRA. Communications between a sender and receiver both within Sweden may not be intercepted; if they cannot be separated, recordings or notes must be destroyed once their domestic nature becomes clear.

The FRA may conduct signals intelligence only under detailed tasking directives issued by certain authorities, and it may not solely target a specific natural person. Permitted purposes include external military threats, international peacekeeping threats, strategic international terrorism or serious cross-border crime, weapons of mass destruction, threats to societal infrastructure, foreign conflicts, foreign intelligence operations against Swedish interests, and certain actions of foreign powers. The FRA also conducts “development activities”. Interception of cable-based signals is automated and uses selectors; selectors directly relating to a specific natural person may be used only if exceptionally important. Permits are issued by the Foreign Intelligence Court, subject to conditions, for maximum six months, renewable. In urgent cases the FRA may grant a permit itself, subject to immediate court review. The court may sit behind closed doors, with a privacy protection representative present.

Intercepted data must be destroyed in certain cases, including data concerning a specific person lacking importance, protected anonymous authorship or media sources, attorney-client privilege, or religious confession. The FRA Personal Data Processing Act and related ordinances regulate personal data, sensitive data, storage, destruction and communication to other authorities or foreign States. Supervision is carried out by the Foreign Intelligence Inspectorate, which conducted 102 inspections from 2009 to 2017, issuing 15 opinions to the FRA and one to the Government; no inspection led to a decision to cease collection or destroy results. Other oversight includes the Privacy Protection Council, data protection officers, the Data Protection Authority, Parliamentary Ombudsmen and the Chancellor of Justice.

Notification of secret surveillance is required if selectors directly related to a specific person were used, but may be delayed for secrecy and need not be given after one year or where measures concern a foreign power. Individuals may ask the Inspectorate to investigate whether their communications were intercepted; 132 requests were handled from 2010 to 2017, with no unlawfulness established. Other remedies include requests to the FRA for information or correction, appeals to the Administrative Court, and damages claims via the Chancellor of Justice. A 2010 Data Protection Authority report was overall positive but noted that notification had never been used due to secrecy considerations.

case_name: CASE OF TSYOGE FON MANTEYFEL v. UKRAINE
summary:
Ms Karina Volodymyrivna Tsyoge fon Manteyfel, a Russian national born in 1978 living in Elektrostal, lodged application no. 29804/16 against Ukraine on 19 May 2016. She was represented by lawyers V. Lebid and M. Tarakhkalo, practising in Kyiv. The application concerns her compulsory psychiatric treatment. She suffers from paranoid schizophrenia and was subject to a court-ordered compulsory medical measure in criminal proceedings in which she had been charged with murder.

From 23 August 2010 to 14 November 2017 the applicant was detained in various psychiatric hospitals under different supervision regimes. During that period the domestic courts periodically reviewed her detention on the basis of submissions from the hospitals and extended her compulsory inpatient treatment. The most recent order for continued compulsory inpatient treatment was issued by the Samarskyy District Court of Dnipropetrovsk on 19 August 2016. According to the applicant, that order expired on 19 February 2017 because the Psychiatric Assistance Act required reviews of such orders at least every six months.

The Dnipro Psychiatric Hospital submitted requests on 13 January and 19 May 2017 for the applicant to continue compulsory inpatient treatment. Those requests were dismissed by the court on 13 May and 2 November 2017 respectively, and the court ordered that she be treated as an outpatient. The applicant was discharged from hospital on 14 November 2017.

The domestic courts did not examine the applicant’s subsequent appeals against the courts’ orders or her requests for release. Under the relevant law at the time, she did not have locus standi to lodge an appeal or initiate a review of the lawfulness of her continued detention. After 19 February 2017, requests for her immediate release lodged by her mother and her lawyer were dismissed by the hospital on the ground that there had been no court decision ordering her release.

In August 2017 the applicant brought a civil claim against the hospital. By a final domestic judgment of 19 June 2019, the Supreme Court partly allowed that claim. It declared that her continued detention after 19 February 2017—after expiry of the six-month period from the 19 August 2016 court decision and in the absence of any further decision extending her detention—had no basis in law. The Supreme Court noted in particular that the Psychiatric Assistance Act’s provision that extension of a compulsory medical measure was to be carried out each time for a period not exceeding six months was a guarantee against unlawful detention. The Supreme Court ordered the Dnipropetrovsk Court of Appeal to rule on the amount of compensation to be awarded to the applicant.

In January 2021 the Dnipropetrovsk Court of Appeal awarded the applicant 30,000 Ukrainian hryvnias for non-pecuniary damage. That judgment was not appealed by the parties and became final. The award remains unpaid to the applicant.
