case_name: CASE OF SHIPS WASTE OIL COLLECTOR B.V. AND OTHERS v. THE NETHERLANDS
summary:
Six Dutch limited-liability companies in two groups complained that intercept data lawfully obtained in criminal investigations had been transmitted to competition authorities and used against them, violating Article 8, and that they lacked an effective domestic remedy under Articles 8 and 13. The first group (Ships Waste Oil Collector B.V., Burando Holding B.V., Port Invest B.V.) collected waste liquids in Rotterdam. The second (Janssen de Jong Groep B.V., Janssen de Jong Infrastructuur Nederland B.V., Janssen de Jong Infra B.V.) operated in construction.

First group: In late 2006 the VROM-IOD began criminal investigation “Toto” into the I. company for suspected forgery and environmental offences. An investigating judge authorised interception of telephone calls by I. employees, including calls with Ships Waste Oil Collector employees; some suggested price-fixing. On 21 October 2008 the public prosecutor approved transmission to the Netherlands Competition Authority (NMA) of a 21 April 2008 official record and transcripts; transmission occurred on 29 June 2009. Further transcripts and recordings were authorised on 23 October 2009. NMA inspectors visited premises on 29–30 June 2010 and questioned managers, playing an intercepted recording. More data were sent in 2010 after approvals in June, July and August; the last transmission was 8–9 September 2010. In the criminal case, the I. company and an employee settled on 11 March 2010 for EUR 50,000 and EUR 4,000; on 5 July 2010 the Rotterdam Regional Court declared the prosecution inadmissible. The NMA’s 28 December 2010 report found collusion from 30 August 2005 to 31 July 2007 contrary to section 6 of the Competition Act. On 16 November 2011 it fined Ships Waste Oil Collector EUR 834,000 and the other three jointly and severally EUR 1,861,000, with Burando’s liability capped at EUR 621,000.

The companies objected that the intercepts were not transmissible “criminal data,” that there was no prior judicial review, that Ships Waste Oil Collector was never suspected, that the settlement prevented ex post facto judicial review, that the NMA lacked intercept powers, and that prior contacts lacked a legal basis. On 11 July 2013 the Rotterdam Regional Court held the data were criminal data but excluded them because the prosecutor’s approvals lacked an identifiable weighing of interests; it quashed the NMA decisions. On 9 July 2015 the Supreme Administrative Court for Trade and Industry quashed that judgment, finding the data qualified as criminal data, a compelling general interest existed, written reasoning was not required, and the transmissions did not breach Article 8. It held the criminal case ended when the 5 July 2010 ruling became final on 19 July 2010. On 20 October 2016 the Regional Court found infringement from 1 January 2006 to 31 July 2007 and reduced fines; on 30 October 2018 the Supreme Administrative Court restored the original fines.

Second group: Around 2007 the “Cleveland” investigation by the Public Prosecution Service and Rijksrecherche examined suspected bribery of local officials; the Janssen companies were suspects. Interceptions were authorised for bribery, fraud and forgery. In July 2008 police gave NMA officials confidential access to transcripts; on 19 August 2008 the prosecutor provided a CD of about thirty recordings for information only. On 9 December 2008 the NMA opened a Competition Act investigation; on 16 December 2008 the prosecutor permitted use of the Cleveland information. Transcripts were transmitted on 24 December 2008. In civil proceedings, the provisional-measures judge on 26 June 2009 dismissed the Janssen companies’ claims, finding the data were criminal data and the transmission compatible with Article 8. NMA reports of 17 December 2009 and 25 February 2010 found infringement; on 29 October 2010 it imposed a EUR 3,000,000 joint fine. The objection was dismissed on 8 March 2012. On 13 June 2013 the Rotterdam Regional Court quashed the decision because no identifiable weighing of interests by the prosecutor existed, although the data were criminal data.
